definition: The revenue and cost attached to a single unit of what a company sells (one customer, one order, one subscription), used to judge whether growth actually makes money.
example: At $12 per order against $15 in delivery and support costs, the unit economics never worked.

definition: A durable advantage such as brand, scale, data or switching costs that keeps rivals from easily winning a firm's customers or profits.
example: Its decade of proprietary payment data is the moat competitors cannot copy.

definition: The speed at which a company spends its cash reserves, usually quoted per month.
example: With a monthly burn rate of $400,000, the startup has eleven months of runway.

definition: The point at which a product satisfies a real and sizeable demand so well that customers pull it forward instead of needing to be pushed.
example: Waiting lists and organic referrals told the team they had finally reached product-market fit.

definition: The single number that best captures the value customers get from a product, used to align a team's priorities.
example: For the budgeting app, weekly active households became the North Star metric.

definition: A framing that explains why people 'hire' a product: by the progress they are trying to make in a given situation, rather than by their demographics.
example: Using jobs to be done, the team realised commuters were hiring the milkshake to make a boring drive less dull.

definition: The accumulated cost of shortcuts in software that make future changes slower and riskier until they are repaid.
example: Skipping the clean-up before launch added technical debt that slowed every later release.

definition: The full revenue opportunity if a product won every possible customer in its category.
example: Investors questioned whether the claimed TAM counted customers who could never afford the product.

definition: A regime in which banks let customers share their account data with licensed third parties through secure APIs.
example: Open banking lets the budgeting app read your balances without ever seeing your password.

definition: Financial services such as payments, credit or insurance offered inside a non-financial company's own app or checkout.
example: The ride-hailing app's instant driver loans are a classic case of embedded finance.

definition: Short-term point-of-sale credit that splits a purchase into instalments, often interest-free for the shopper.
example: Regulators are asking whether BNPL schemes hide how much households really owe.

definition: Software that helps firms meet regulatory obligations, such as monitoring, reporting and identity checks, with less manual effort.
example: The bank cut its onboarding time in half after adopting a RegTech identity-verification tool.

definition: The difference between the tax a government should collect under the law and what it actually collects.
example: Better data matching is one way tax agencies hope to narrow the tax gap.

definition: Strategies that move taxable profit to low-tax places where little real activity occurs; the target of a major OECD reform programme.
example: The new reporting rules were designed to curb BEPS by large multinationals.

definition: The prices charged for goods, services or intellectual property exchanged between related companies in different countries, which tax rules expect to match what unrelated parties would agree.
example: The audit questioned the transfer pricing on royalties paid to the group's overseas arm.

definition: The OECD framework for a 15 per cent global minimum tax on large multinational groups.
example: Finance teams are updating their systems to calculate effective tax rates for Pillar Two.

definition: Issuing invoices as structured digital data exchanged through approved systems, often reported to tax authorities in near real time.
example: Mandatory e-invoicing means the tax portal sees the sale before the customer pays.

definition: Handling a transaction from start to finish electronically, with no manual intervention.
example: Straight-through processing cut settlement errors because nobody re-typed the trade details.

definition: Comparing groups of users who share a starting point, such as signup month, to see how their behaviour changes over time.
example: Cohort analysis showed that customers who joined in spring stayed far longer than winter signups.

definition: The simplest version of a product that lets a team learn from real users with the least effort.
example: Their MVP was a single web form and a spreadsheet behind it.

definition: Objectives and Key Results: a goal-setting method that pairs an ambitious aim with a few measurable results.
example: The quarterly OKRs made it clear which projects mattered and which could wait.

definition: Ongoing work to clarify, size and order upcoming items so the team always has well-understood work ready to start.
example: A short weekly backlog refinement meant sprint planning no longer ran for three hours.

definition: A short description of a need from the user's viewpoint, usually written as 'As a..., I want..., so that...'.
example: The user story read: as a taxpayer, I want to upload receipts from my phone so that filing takes minutes.

definition: The specific conditions a piece of work must meet before it is accepted as done.
example: Clear acceptance criteria stopped the argument about whether the export feature was finished.

definition: Charting the people affected by or influencing a project by their interest and power, to decide how to engage each of them.
example: Stakeholder mapping revealed that the compliance team had a veto nobody had planned for.

definition: Comparing the current state with the desired state to identify what must change to close the difference.
example: The gap analysis showed the finance system could not produce the new regulatory report.

definition: A structured list of a business's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats.
example: Their SWOT analysis listed a loyal customer base as a strength and one-supplier dependence as a threat.

definition: A chart assigning each task to the people who are Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed.
example: The RACI matrix settled who signs off on pricing changes.

definition: A deliberate change in a startup's direction based on what it has learned, while keeping its core insights.
example: After lukewarm sales to consumers, the company pivoted to selling its software to accountants.

definition: The way a product becomes more valuable to each user as more people use it.
example: A payments app is only useful if your friends and local shops are on it too, which is a network effect.

definition: Markets organised around digital platforms that connect producers and consumers and earn a fee or commission on the matches.
example: Freelancers in the platform economy depend on a few apps for most of their work.

definition: A self-reinforcing loop in which each success makes the next one easier, such as more sellers attracting more buyers who attract more sellers.
example: Lower prices brought more shoppers, which brought more sellers, and the flywheel kept spinning.

definition: Cutting out the middleman so that producers deal directly with customers.
example: Direct-to-consumer brands grew by disintermediation of the traditional retailer.

definition: Splitting a bundled offering into separate services that specialists can do better, as fintech firms did to banks.
example: The unbundling of the bank left one app for savings, another for transfers and a third for loans.

definition: The time, money or effort a customer must spend to move from one provider to another.
example: High switching costs keep businesses on their accounting software even when a cheaper tool appears.

definition: How much profit swings for a given change in sales, which depends on how much of a firm's cost base is fixed.
example: With high operating leverage, a small rise in sales lifted profit sharply.

definition: The rate at which customers or subscribers stop buying or cancel.
example: Monthly churn fell from five per cent to three after the onboarding redesign.

definition: The yearly value of a company's subscription contracts, normalised to a twelve-month figure.
example: Crossing $10 million in ARR made the firm eligible for the growth-stage fund.

definition: A supervised space in which firms can test new financial products under eased rules for a limited time.
example: The lender trialled its AI credit model inside the regulator's sandbox before a full launch.

definition: A small change in how choices are presented that steers behaviour without removing any options.
example: Pre-filling the tax form with last year's details was a gentle nudge toward filing early.
